## Overview

The paper estimates the parameters by Bayesian inference under uniform priors, with two
samplers: a component-wise Metropolis–Hastings algorithm and adaptive multiple importance
sampling (AMIS). This vignette builds the posterior of the paper's reduced model and runs
short versions of both, then shows the Turing.jl interface. A likelihood takes about a
second, so the runs here are far too short for real estimates; they show the workflow.

## Setup

```{julia}
using AshDieback
using AbstractMCMC
using MCMCChains
using LinearAlgebra
using LogDensityProblems
using Random
using Plots

data = load_peoc_data()
θ0 = AshDiebackParameters([1000.0, 0.0, 24.0, 0.0, 18.0, 90.0, 21.50001, 1.0, 0.0085, 0.05])
prob = AshDiebackProblem(data, θ0)
```

## The posterior

The reduced model (eq. 13 of the paper) has no Allee effect and no rainfall effect, fixes
γ and C_pers, and estimates β₀, D, S, C_init and κ:

```{julia}
post = AshDiebackPosterior(prob, reduced_model_prior_ranges())
free_parameters(post)
```

`post` is a LogDensityProblems.jl log density over the free parameters:

```{julia}
x0 = θ0[post.free]
LogDensityProblems.logdensity(post, x0)
```

## Metropolis–Hastings

PEOC's sampler updates one parameter per iteration with a gamma proposal centred on its
current value (shape 200, so a standard deviation of 7 % of the value):

```{julia}
spl = ComponentwiseGammaMH(post)
chain = sample(Xoshiro(1), post, spl, 200; initial_params = x0, chain_type = Chains,
               progress = false)
```

Trace plots of three of the parameters (MCMCChains' default plot adds density plots, which
need StatsPlots.jl):

```{julia}
plot(chain[:, [:beta_0, :D, :S_sat], 1]; seriestype = :traceplot, size = (800, 600))
```

## AMIS

AMIS draws batches from a Gaussian proposal, weights all draws so far against the mixture
of the proposals used, and moves the proposal to the weighted mean and covariance. The
paper's initial proposal for the T28 index (its Table 2) has these variances:

```{julia}
Σ0 = Diagonal([3.0, 0.4, 1.0, 1e-8, 1.5e-5])
res = amis(Xoshiro(2), post, x0, Matrix(Σ0); iterations = 3, samples = 40)
res.means[end]
```

With several threads (`julia --threads=auto`) the likelihoods of a batch are evaluated in
parallel.

## Turing

`turing_model(post)` gives the same posterior as a Turing.jl model, so Turing's samplers
and tools apply. The likelihood has no useful gradient, so use a gradient-free sampler:

```{julia}
using Turing
model = turing_model(post)
Turing.DynamicPPL.logjoint(model, (; θ = x0)) ≈ LogDensityProblems.logdensity(post, x0)
```
